1	---
2	name: review-request
3	description: 別セッションで実行する上流レビュー (code-review など) の依頼文を、雛形から埋めてファイルに書き出す。結果の出力先を依頼文に埋め込み、新しいセッションには依頼文のパス 1 つを渡す。「レビューの依頼文を作って」「再レビューの依頼文をください」「review-request を実行して」のような依頼で使う。引数でスキル名 (省略時は code-review)・モデル名・effort と、依頼文と結果のディレクトリ (--dir。省略時は tmp/) を指定する。記録に回があっても全量の依頼文を作るには --full-review を、全量の起点にする派生元のブランチは --base を付ける。レビュアに依頼元と別の作業ツリーを読ませるときは、その作業ツリーを --target-dir で指定する。
4	---
5	
6	# review-request: レビューの依頼文の生成
7	
8	別セッションで実行する上流レビューの依頼文を、雛形 ([review-request-template.md](../review-triage/references/review-request-template.md)) を埋めてファイルに書き出す。**成果物は依頼文のファイル 1 つで、レビューは実行しない。** 実行するのは人間で、新しいセッションに依頼文のパスを渡す。結果を受け取って判定するのは [review-triage](../review-triage/SKILL.md)。
9	
10	依頼の運用 (なぜファイルに書き出すか・範囲の規則・各節の理由) の SSOT (single source of truth。ある事実を定めている唯一の記述) は [review-request.md](../review-triage/references/review-request.md)。ここでは言い直さない。
11	
12	## 引数
13	
14	```
15	review-request [<スキル名>] [<モデル名>] [<effort>] [--dir <ディレクトリ>] [--full-review] [--base <ブランチ>] [--target-dir <ディレクトリ>]
16	```
17	
18	| 引数 | 意味 | 省略時 |
19	| --- | --- | --- |
20	| `<スキル名>` | 依頼文でレビュアに呼ばせるレビュースキル | 手順 1 |
21	| `<モデル名>` | レビューを実行するモデル | 手順 1 |
22	| `<effort>` | レビュースキルに渡す effort | 手順 1 |
23	| `--dir <ディレクトリ>` | 依頼文と結果のディレクトリ。相対パスはリポジトリのルート (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`) を基準に解決する。作業ツリーの外は受け付けない (git に無視されていることを確認できないため) | `tmp/` |
24	| `--full-review` | 記録に回があっても、範囲を全量 (scope `full`) にする。要否に関わらず全量にする明示の指定 (要否の規則の SSOT は [review-request.md](../review-triage/references/review-request.md) の「収束後の全量レビューと、その要否」) | 範囲は手順 2 のとおり (記録に回が無ければ全量、あれば増分) |
25	| `--base <ブランチ>` | 全量の起点を求める派生元のブランチ (別の作業ブランチから派生したブランチなら、その作業ブランチ)。増分の回では使わない | `origin/HEAD` が指すブランチ (手順 2) |
26	| `--target-dir <ディレクトリ>` | 依頼文の「対象」の作業ツリー (レビュアが読む作業ツリー)。依頼元と同じリポジトリの worktree のルートを、絶対パスか、リポジトリのルートからの相対パスで渡す。依頼元はこの作業ツリーを、依頼文の `head` に合わせ、レビューの間は変えずに保つ (このスキルはその作業ツリーの HEAD と clean を確認しない。手順 1) | 依頼元の作業ツリー (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`) |
27	
28	位置引数はこの順で読む。`--dir`・`--full-review`・`--base`・`--target-dir` は位置引数の前後どちらに置いてもよい。`--full-review` と `--base` は設定のキーを持たない。どちらもブランチやループごとに変わる値である。ループのディレクトリに依頼文を書くスキル (`review-loop`・`review-rally`) が、`--dir` を毎回、`--base` を全量の回に使う。`--full-review` を使うのは `review-loop` と `review-rally`、`--target-dir` を毎回使うのは `review-rally` である。`--target-dir` も設定のキーを持たない。どの作業ツリーを読ませるかは、依頼ごとに依頼元が決めるためである。
29	
30	## 前提知識
31	
32	- **依頼文を会話に貼らない。** 貼り方が回ごとに変わると、出力先の名前・様式・読み取り専用の条件も回ごとに変わる (理由と実測は [review-request.md](../review-triage/references/review-request.md))。出力先のパスは生成の時点で依頼文に埋め込まれるので、レビュアがそこをずらす余地が無い。
33	- **雛形の各節 (作業ツリーの扱い・報告前の検証・報告しない条件・出力様式) はそのまま写す。** 生成のたびに言い直さない。言い直すと、貼り方が回ごとに変わる元の問題に戻る。
34	- **スキル名とモデル名は推測しない。** 記録の `skill` / `model` にそのまま入るので、依頼したものと違う値が記録に残ると、粒度の比較が成り立たなくなる。
35	
36	## 手順
37	
38	1. **引数と設定を読む**: 引数はスキル名・モデル名・effort とディレクトリ (様式は上の「引数」)。**スキル名の省略時は `code-review`。モデル名は、引数に無ければ設定 (`.claude/akm-claude-plugins/review-triage/config.json`) の `loop.review_model` を使い、それも未設定なら人間に質問する。effort は、引数に無ければ設定の `loop.review_args`、それも未設定なら既定 (SSOT は [review-invocation.md](../review-triage-loop/references/review-invocation.md) の「effort の既定」)。`ce-code-review` のように effort を受け取らない skill では空にする** (設定のキーの SSOT は [project-config.md](../review-triage/references/project-config.md))。あわせて設定の `record_dir` を読む (未設定なら既定の `tmp/review-triages/`)。
39	   - **`--target-dir` があれば、そのディレクトリが依頼元と同じリポジトリの worktree のルートであることを確認する。** `git -C <ディレクトリ> rev-parse --show-toplevel` がそのディレクトリ自身の実体パスで、`git -C <ディレクトリ> rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir` が依頼元の同じ値と一致すれば、同じリポジトリの worktree のルートである。当たらなければ生成せず、その旨を報告して終了する。別のリポジトリや worktree の中のディレクトリを対象にした依頼文は、範囲 (手順 2) の `base` と `head` のコミットがレビュアの作業ツリーに無いか、レビュアがリポジトリの一部しか読まないことになり、どちらもレビューの結果からは気づけない。
40	   - **`--target-dir` の作業ツリーの HEAD と clean は確認しない。** 依頼文の `head` に合わせることと、レビューの間に変えないことは、その作業ツリーを用意した依頼元が受け持つ。このスキルが確認すると、依頼元が作業ツリーを合わせる前に依頼文を作る使い方ができなくなる。依頼元の作業ツリーの確認 (手順 2) は、`--target-dir` があっても行う。
41	2. **回と範囲を決める**: 現在のブランチの記録 (`<record_dir>/<ブランチ名>.yaml`。ブランチ名の `/` は `-` に置き換える) を読み、`runs` の数 + 1 を回とする (記録が無ければ 1)。**記録があるのに読めない (YAML として壊れている・`runs` が無い) なら、生成せずにその旨を報告して終了する。** 「読めない」を「無い」に寄せると回の番号が 1 から振り直され、過去の回と同じ番号の依頼文ができる。
42	   - **記録に回が無いか、引数 `--full-review` があれば、scope は `full`。** `base` は、起点のブランチと HEAD の merge-base (共通祖先のコミット) の短縮 SHA (`git merge-base <ブランチ> HEAD` の結果を `git rev-parse --short` で縮めたもの)。起点のブランチは、引数 `--base` があればそれ、無ければ `origin/HEAD` が指すブランチ (`git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` の結果。`origin/main` のような形のまま使う)。起点を分岐元の `main` に決め打ちしないのは、別の作業ブランチから派生したブランチで、派生元のコミットまで範囲に入るため。**`--base` のブランチが解決できない (`git rev-parse --verify --quiet "<ブランチ>^{commit}"` が失敗する)、`--base` が無くて `origin/HEAD` が無い、または merge-base が求まらない (共通祖先が無い) なら、生成せずにその旨を報告し、起点のブランチをどれにするかを人間に質問する。** 起点を推測すると、範囲が広すぎるか狭すぎる依頼文ができ、どちらもレビューの結果からは気づけない。
43	     - 補足は、記録に回が無く `--full-review` も無ければ「ブランチの全量 (起点: `<ブランチ>` との merge-base)」。`--full-review` があれば「ブランチの全量 (`--full-review` による指定。起点: `<ブランチ>` との merge-base)。増分の外を報告しない規則はこの回には当てはまらない」。書き分けるのは、記録に回がある状態の全量の回で、レビュアが前の回の依頼文にあった増分の規則をこの回に当てはめないようにするため。
44	   - **それ以外 (記録に回があり、`--full-review` が無い) なら、scope は `incremental`、`base` は直前の回の `head`。** `--base` は使わない (あっても無視し、報告にその旨を書く)。補足は「前回の HEAD `<sha>` からの増分。増分の外は、増分が壊した場合のみ報告する」。
45	   - **ディレクトリ (`--dir`。省略時は `tmp/`) が `git check-ignore -q <ディレクトリ>` で無視されていなければ生成せず、「`.gitignore` にディレクトリ (既定なら `tmp/`) を足してコミットしてから再実行する」と案内して終了する。** スキルは `.gitignore` を変えない。依頼文と結果は設定の `record_dir` に関わらずこのディレクトリに置くので、記録のディレクトリと違って「既定のディレクトリを使うとき」に限らず常に確認する (前提の SSOT は [record-schema.md](../review-triage/references/record-schema.md) の冒頭)。`git check-ignore` は存在しないパスでも判定できるので、ディレクトリを作る前に確認する。
46	   - `head` は現在の HEAD の短縮 SHA。**作業ツリーが clean でなければ生成せず、その旨を報告する。** 依頼文は作業ツリーの扱いを「共有」(依頼元の作業ツリーか `--target-dir` の作業ツリーを、読み取り専用でレビューする) で書くので、レビュアは HEAD と作業ツリーが不変であることを確認して報告する。汚れたまま渡すと、その確認が成り立たない。ループ (`review-loop`) で「使い捨て」に書き換えた依頼文でも、依頼元の作業ツリーは確認する (確認するのはワーカーで、SSOT は [review-loop の worker.md](../review-loop/references/worker.md) の「回の処理」の手順 4)。
47	3. **識別子と出力先を決める**: 識別子は `<YYYYMMDD>-<hhmm>-<ブランチ名>-<回>-<スキル名>-<モデル名>`。依頼文は `<ディレクトリ>/review-request-<識別子>.md`、レビュー結果の出力先は `<ディレクトリ>/review-<識別子>.yaml` (ディレクトリの既定は `tmp/`)。成分ごとの扱いは下の表が SSOT で、**成分を足す・外す・変えるときは、その行の全欄を確認する。** 欄を 1 つ書き残すと、その扱いが無いことは次のレビューまで気づかれない (実測: 成分を変えるたびに、外した成分の役割・足した成分の整え方・参照先の規則、と別の欄で 3 回続いた)。識別子はファイル名に使うので、整え方はファイル名に使える形にするためのもの。識別子の衝突 (同じ名前の依頼文か結果が既にある状態) は 1 つずつやり直せるので、厳密な一意性は求めない。
48	
49	   | 成分 | 出所 | 整え方 | 欠損時の扱い | なぜ入れるか |
50	   | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
51	   | 日時 (`YYYYMMDD-hhmm`) | 生成した日時 | 数字だけなのでそのまま | — (必ず取れる) | 先頭に置くと一覧が時系列に並ぶ |
52	   | ブランチ名 | 現在のブランチ | `/` と、ファイル名に使えない文字を `-` に置き換える (記録の YAML のファイル名の規則とは別に定める。参照しない) | detached HEAD なら `detached-<短縮 SHA>` | `tmp/` は手元にしか無く、同じリポジトリの別のブランチで同じ回を回すと衝突する (実測) |
53	   | 回 | 手順 2 | 数字だけなのでそのまま | 記録が無ければ 1。記録があるのに読めなければ生成せず報告して終了 (手順 2) | 同じブランチの過去の回と区別する |
54	   | スキル名・モデル名 | 手順 1 | `/` と、ファイル名に使えない文字を `-` に置き換える (設定や引数の表記をそのまま入れない) | 未指定なら手順 1 の既定か人間に質問する | 同じ回に複数のレビュアでレビューを実行したとき (同じ分に作れば日時は同じ) を分け、依頼文を開かずにどのレビュアの結果かが分かる |
55	
56	   - **どちらかが既に存在すれば上書きせず、その旨を報告して終了する。** 同じ識別子で作り直したいときは人間が消す。
57	4. **雛形を埋めて書き出す**: 雛形の `{{…}}` は、`repo` (`git remote get-url origin`)・`repo_dir` (`--target-dir` があればその作業ツリーのルートの絶対パス、無ければ `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`)・`branch` (現在のブランチ名)・`base` / `head` / `scope` / `scope_note` (手順 2)・`skill` / `model` / `effort` (手順 1)・`date` (生成日 `YYYY-MM-DD`)・`run_id` (手順 3 の識別子)・`output_path` (手順 3 の出力先を、依頼元の作業ツリーのルート (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`) 起点の絶対パスにしたもの。`--dir` の相対パスの基準と同じで、`--target-dir` があっても変えない) で埋める。ディレクトリが無ければ作る (無視されていることは手順 2 で確認済み)。
58	   - **出力先は絶対パスで埋める。** 相対パスはレビュアの cwd (作業ディレクトリ) で解決され、別の場所に書かれた実測がある。
59	   - **雛形の「対象」の節にある作業ツリーの扱いの行 (`- 作業ツリーの扱い: 共有`) は書き換えず、値「共有」のまま書く。** 「使い捨て」への書き換えはループ (`review-loop`) のワーカーが行う (SSOT は [review-loop の worker.md](../review-loop/references/worker.md) の「回の処理」の手順 8)。
60	   - **依頼文は、同じディレクトリの一時名 `.review-request-<識別子>.md.tmp` に書き、埋め残した `{{…}}` が無いことを確認してから、`mv` で `review-request-<識別子>.md` に改名する。** ディレクトリを定期的に確認するプロセス (`review-loop` のワーカー) は一時名 (`.` で始まる名前) を読まないので、書きかけの依頼文を処理しない。
61	5. **報告する**: 依頼文のパスと出力先のパス、埋めた値 (対象・範囲・スキル名・モデル名・effort) を出す。**`--target-dir` があれば、対象の作業ツリーのパスと、その作業ツリーの HEAD と clean を確認していないことも出す** (手順 1)。**scope が `full` なら、起点のブランチ名と merge-base の SHA、ブランチの出所 (`--base` か、`origin/HEAD` による既定か)、`--full-review` の有無も出す。** 起点を推測しない規則を、人間が報告で確認できるようにするため。**新しいセッションへ渡すのは依頼文のパス 1 つ**であること、結果が返ったら `review-triage` に出力先のパスを渡すことを案内する。
62	
63	## 原則
64	
65	- **レビューを実行しない。** 実行するかどうか、どのセッションで実行するかは人間が決める。
66	- **既存の依頼文・結果を上書きしない。** 回の途中で作り直すと、どの結果がどの依頼に対応するかが辿れなくなる。
67	- **依頼文のファイルはコミットしない。** このディレクトリに置き、記録と同じく git の追跡外にする (無視されていなければ手順 2 で終了する)。
68	
69	## このスキルがしないこと
70	
71	- **レビュー結果の様式の検査** — 受け取るスキル (`review-triage` の手順 1) が担う。

content.text:
#170 の計画を書く前に、対象の範囲を確認してください。文書を読み直した結果、計画はまだ書いていません。

## 計画の範囲

スキル `review-rally` とスキル `review-request` の文書を変更し、呼び出し元のセッションが worktree で動く場合も、メインの作業ツリーで動く場合も、同じ手順で動くようにします。README の説明と、プラグインの版の更新も含めます。

スキル `review-loop` のワーカーは変更しません。

## 決定済みのこと

[akm/claude-plugins#170](https://github.com/akm/claude-plugins/issues/170) の「検討の結果」の 1〜5 に従います。

- 依頼文は呼び出し元のセッションの作業ツリーに、結果はレビューの worktree に書き、絶対パスで渡す
- レビューの worktree の HEAD は、レビューのセッションが切り替える
- ブランチの一覧の突き合わせでは、メインの作業ツリー以外の worktree がチェックアウトしていたブランチを除く
- メインの作業ツリーの HEAD が指すブランチの名前も比べる
- 語を「呼び出し元のセッション」に変え、#151 の計画は変えない

## 確認していただきたい 4 つの点

**1. 結果の書き込み先の指定**

`review-request` に引数を足しません。既存の引数 `--target-dir` (レビュアが読む作業ツリーの指定) があるときは、結果をその作業ツリーの、依頼文と同じ相対パスに書く形にします。指定は増えませんが、この引数の意味が変わります。

あわせて、結果のディレクトリが git に無視されているかの確認は、呼び出し元のセッションの作業ツリーでの 1 回だけにします。相対パスとコミットが同じなので、判定も同じになるためです。前に「レビューのセッションが切り替えの後に確認する」と説明した点の変更です。

**2. レビューの worktree が clean でないとき、または切り替えに失敗したとき**

レビューのセッションが `failed` で報告し、レビュー不成立 (停止ノード RR1) として停止します。今は「レビューのセッションを使えない」(停止ノード RR2) です。呼び出し元のセッションが事前にも確認する案は、確認が 2 か所になるので採りません。

**3. 通し確認の方法**

マージの前に、worktree で動くセッションが、ブランチの文書を直接読んで手順を実行します。インストール済みのプラグインは古い版なので、Skill ツールでは新しい手順を読めないためです。メインの作業ツリーで動くセッションからも、少なくとも 1 回のレビューを確認します。

実行の前に、回数・費用・手順をお見せして許可をいただきます。

権限モードは auto だけで確認し、ほかのモードは未確認と記録します。レビューのセッションが依頼文を読むときも、呼び出し元のセッションが結果を読むときも、自分の作業ツリーの外を読むことになります。auto 以外のモードでは、ここが承認待ちになる可能性があります。

**4. `stops.md` の片付けの案内**

ファイル `review-triage/skills/review-rally/references/stops.md` の「アーカイブで worktree も片付けられる」は、今回の計画に含めず、別の Issue にします。アーカイブの後に worktree がどう扱われるかの調査が要り、worktree のセッションへの対応とは動機も違うためです。

直す点がある場合は、番号と内容を教えてください。
この内容で進める
計画を書きます。スキル `ce-plan` の残りの手順を読み、既存の計画の書式も確認します。

48	**Slack context** (opt-in) — never auto-dispatch. Route by condition:
49	
50	- **Tools available + user asked**: Dispatch a generic subagent with `references/agents/slack-researcher.md` and the planning context summary in parallel with other Phase 1.1 agents. If the origin document has a Slack context section, pass it verbatim so the researcher focuses on gaps. Include findings in consolidation.
51	- **Tools available + user didn't ask**: Note in output: "Slack tools detected. Ask me to search Slack for organizational context at any point, or include it in your next prompt."
52	- **No tools + user asked**: Note in output: "Slack context was requested but no Slack tools are available. Install and authenticate the Slack plugin to enable organizational context search."
53	
54	#### 1.1b Detect Execution Direction Signals
55	
56	Decide whether the plan should carry a lightweight execution direction signal.
57	
58	Look for signals such as:
59	- The user explicitly asks for TDD, test-first, or characterization-first work
60	- The origin document calls for test-first implementation or exploratory hardening of legacy code
61	- Local research shows the target area is legacy, weakly tested, or historically fragile, suggesting characterization coverage before changing behavior
62	- The work is mostly configuration, packaging, UI styling, or environment setup where the right first proof is a smoke/runtime check rather than unit coverage
63	
64	When the signal is clear, carry it forward silently in the relevant implementation units.
65	
66	Ask the user only if the direction would materially change sequencing or risk and cannot be responsibly inferred.
67	
68	#### 1.2 Decide on External Research
69	
70	Based on the origin document, user signals, and local findings, decide **whether** external research adds value and, if so, **what kind**. Resolve this in three stages: explicit-request priority, intent classification, then the implicit signals below.
71	
72	**Stage 1 — An explicit request takes precedence.** If the user prompt **or** the origin requirements document explicitly asks for external input — a signal that the answer lives outside the repo, such as competitor/prior-art comparison, "what should we borrow", "from the web", "best practices", "official docs", "alternatives to", a market scan, or naming a specific external technology to consult — external research is **required**, regardless of how strong local patterns look. The list is illustrative; key on the signal, not the exact phrase — any wording that clearly points outside the repo qualifies. The skip conditions below do **not** apply to an explicit request. The only thing that overrides it is an explicit opt-out ("no web research", "skip external research"): honor that, skip, and note it. Improvement or quality verbs ("improve", "make better") carry no external signal on their own and never trigger research by themselves.
73	
74	**Stage 2 — Classify the research intent** (whenever external research will run, from Stage 1 or the implicit signals below) so Phase 1.3 routes correctly. Use this mechanical test, not a fixed phrase list:
75	- **Implementation-guidance** — the approach or technology is already settled; the question is *how to build it well* (best practices, version-specific docs, API constraints, known pitfalls, deprecations).
76	- **Landscape / option-discovery** — the question is *what options or prior art exist* (competitor scans, build-vs-buy, library/provider selection, prior art, market signals, cross-domain analogies).
77	- **Mixed** — both: discover an unsettled external option set first, then research the shortlisted choice for implementation guidance.
78	
79	**Stage 3 — Implicit signals** decide the call when no explicit request fired.
80	
81	**Read between the lines.** Pay attention to signals from the conversation so far:
82	- **User familiarity** — Are they pointing to specific files or patterns? They likely know the codebase well.
83	- **User intent** — Do they want speed or thoroughness? Exploration or execution?
84	- **Topic risk** — Security, payments, external APIs warrant more caution regardless of user signals.
85	- **Uncertainty level** — Is the approach clear or still open-ended?
86	
87	**Leverage the repo research prompt's technology context:**
88	
89	Use technology facts already present in the project's active instructions, planning context, or task-specific repo research. Read any exact version fresh from the owning manifest when it materially affects an external-research decision:
90	
91	- If specific frameworks and versions were detected (e.g., Rails 7.2, Next.js 14, Go 1.22), pass those exact identifiers to the `framework-docs-researcher` local prompt so it fetches version-specific documentation
92	- If the feature touches a technology layer the scan found well-established in the repo (e.g., existing Sidekiq jobs when planning a new background job), lean toward skipping external research -- local patterns are likely sufficient
93	- If the feature touches a technology layer the scan found absent or thin (e.g., no existing proto files when planning a new gRPC service), lean toward external research -- there are no local patterns to follow
94	- If the scan detected deployment infrastructure (Docker, K8s, serverless), note it in the planning context passed to downstream agents so they can account for deployment constraints
95	- If the scan detected a monorepo and scoped to a specific service, pass that service's tech context to downstream research agents -- not the aggregate of all services. If the scan surfaced the workspace map without scoping, use the feature description to identify the relevant service before proceeding with research
96	
97	**Always lean toward external research when:**
98	- The topic is high-risk: security, payments, privacy, external APIs, migrations, compliance
99	- The codebase lacks relevant local patterns -- fewer than 3 direct examples of the pattern this plan needs
100	- Local patterns exist for an adjacent domain but not the exact one -- e.g., the codebase has HTTP clients but not webhook receivers, or has background jobs but not event-driven pub/sub. Adjacent patterns suggest the team is comfortable with the technology layer but may not know domain-specific pitfalls. When this signal is present, frame the external research query around the domain gap specifically, not the general technology
101	- The user is exploring unfamiliar territory
102	- The technology scan found the relevant layer absent or thin in the codebase
103	- The plan's recommendations depend on a genuinely external, **unsettled** option set — which library, provider, or approach to adopt, or what competitors and prior art do — **even when local implementation patterns are strong** (intent: landscape). Bound this implicit landscape trigger by three gates: (a) the option set genuinely lives outside the repo, (b) the decision materially shapes the plan (a KTD, dependency, or architecture choice — not an incidental detail), and (c) no settled local or team choice already exists. Improvement verbs alone never satisfy this.
104	
105	**Skip external research when** (only when Stage 1 found no explicit request — an explicit request is never skipped):
106	- The codebase already shows a strong local pattern -- multiple direct examples (not adjacent-domain), recently touched, following current conventions
107	- The user already knows the intended shape
108	- Additional external context would add little practical value
109	- The technology scan found the relevant layer well-established with existing examples to follow
110	
111	When an explicit request *did* fire but a settled local or team choice already exists, **narrow the research rather than skipping it** — research the current pitfalls, docs, and practices for the chosen library/pattern instead of re-surveying the whole option set.
112	
113	Announce the decision and the intent briefly before continuing. Examples:
114	- "Your codebase has solid patterns for this. Proceeding without external research."
115	- "This involves payment processing, so I'll research current best practices first (implementation-guidance)."
116	- "You asked what to borrow from competitors, so I'll run a landscape scan first (landscape/option-discovery)."
117	
118	#### 1.3 External Research (Conditional)
119	
120	If Step 1.2 indicates external research is useful, dispatch by the **intent** classified in Stage 2, using the platform's subagent primitive (`Agent`/`Task` in Claude Code, `spawn_agent` in Codex) where available; otherwise run the work inline or serially. Read the selected prompt asset from `references/agents/` and seed a generic subagent with it. For `web-researcher.md`, pass a focus hint plus the planning context summary and do **not** pass codebase content — it operates externally.
121	
122	- **Implementation-guidance** — run in parallel:
123	  - `references/agents/best-practices-researcher.md` with the planning context summary.
124	  - `references/agents/framework-docs-researcher.md` with the planning context summary and exact frameworks/versions from Phase 1.1 where available.
125	- **Landscape / option-discovery** — `references/agents/web-researcher.md` with the focus hint and planning context summary. When the request targets projects on a code host (e.g., "competitors on GitHub"), name the discovery dimensions in the focus hint: project names and URLs, release recency and activity, CLI/UX shape, install path, docs and examples, plugin/extension surfaces, recurring issue themes, and license — treating star counts as a weak signal only.
126	- **Mixed** — **sequential, not parallel**: run the `web-researcher` local prompt first to map the landscape and produce a shortlist; then run the `framework-docs-researcher` and/or `best-practices-researcher` local prompts against the shortlisted technologies only when their details materially shape the plan.
127	
128	**Tool-unavailable handling.** `web-researcher` self-checks for web tools and stops if they are missing. Never block on this: if it reports research unavailable, or any researcher fails, warn and proceed, and carry the gap into Phase 1.4 so the plan records it honestly — especially when the user explicitly requested external research, where a silent skip would leave the plan looking evidence-based when it is not.
129	
130	#### 1.4 Consolidate Research
131	
132	Summarize:
133	- Relevant codebase patterns and file paths
134	- Relevant institutional learnings
135	- Organizational context from Slack conversations, if gathered (prior discussions, decisions, or domain knowledge relevant to the feature)
136	- External references, prior art, competitor/landscape findings, and best practices, if gathered
137	- Related issues, PRs, or prior art
138	- Any constraints that should materially shape the plan
139	
140	**Land external findings in decisions, not an appendix.** Any external research that ran must surface where it changes a choice — Key Technical Decisions rationale, Alternatives, Risks, or Sources & Research — not as a detached list with no bearing on the plan. If a finding shaped nothing, it was not load-bearing; do not pad the plan with it.
141	
142	**Mark whether external research was load-bearing.** Record a single internal flag: did external findings materially shape a KTD, Alternative, Scope boundary, or Risk? This flag answers only that question — it does **not** gate whether research runs (Phase 1.2 owns that decision). Phase 5.3.2 reads it to decide whether to enter a confidence-scoring pass.
143	
144	**Record requested-but-unavailable.** If the user explicitly requested external research but it could not run (web tools unavailable, researcher failed), state that in the plan as an assumption or open question rather than presenting the plan as externally grounded.
145	
146	#### 1.4b Reclassify Depth When Research Reveals External Contract Surfaces
147	
148	If the current classification is **Lightweight** and Phase 1 research found that the work touches any of these external contract surfaces, reclassify to **Standard**:
149	
150	- Environment variables consumed by external systems, CI, or other repositories
151	- Exported public APIs, CLI flags, or command-line interface contracts
152	- CI/CD configuration files (`.github/workflows/`, `Dockerfile`, deployment scripts)
153	- Shared types or interfaces imported by downstream consumers
154	- Documentation referenced by external URLs or linked from other systems
155	
156	This ensures flow analysis (Phase 1.5) runs and the confidence check (Phase 5.3) applies critical-section bonuses. Announce the reclassification briefly: "Reclassifying to Standard — this change touches [environment variables / exported APIs / CI config] with external consumers."
157	
158	#### 1.5 Flow and Edge-Case Analysis (Conditional)
159	
160	For **Standard** or **Deep** plans, or when user flow completeness is still unclear, run:
161	
162	- `references/agents/spec-flow-analyzer.md` with the planning context summary and research findings.
163	
164	Use the output to:
165	- Identify missing edge cases, state transitions, or handoff gaps
166	- Tighten requirements trace or verification strategy
167	- Add only the flow details that materially improve the plan

1	# Structure and Write the Plan
2	
3	Phase 2 through 4 of `ce-plan`. Read this before building the planning-question list.
4	
5	### Phase 2: Resolve Planning Questions
6	
7	Build a planning question list from:
8	- Deferred questions in the origin document
9	- Gaps discovered in repo or external research
10	- Technical decisions required to produce a useful plan
11	
12	For each question, decide whether it should be:
13	- **Resolved during planning** - the answer is knowable from repo context, documentation, or user choice
14	- **Deferred to implementation** - the answer depends on code changes, runtime behavior, or execution-time discovery
15	
16	Ask the user only when the answer materially affects architecture, scope, sequencing, or risk and cannot be responsibly inferred. Use the platform's blocking question tool when available (see Interaction Method).
17	
18	**Never re-ask a session-settled decision.** A decision carrying the `session-settled:` label, or classified settled per `references/settled-decisions.md`, is answered input, not a planning question. An unexamined directive receives exactly one challenge here, backed by research evidence, and the outcome lands in the plan as a labeled or unlabeled Key Technical Decision — the plan is the challenge ledger; later pipeline stages do not re-challenge. An unanswered pipeline-surfaced challenge resurfaces only through the calling pipeline's residual channel.
19	
20	**Scaffold questions on unfamiliar territory.** When the user has signaled they lack working knowledge of the area a question lives in — an explicit "I don't know X", or earlier answers showing they *cannot evaluate* options rather than merely haven't decided — do not ask the question naked. Present it as a taught decision: the realistic options, one clause each on the trade-off that matters for this plan, and a recommended default. If the user still cannot evaluate, record the default as an explicit assumption in the plan instead of extracting a guess. In pipeline mode (LFG, any `disable-model-invocation` context) this scaffolding never presents anything — resolve to the recommended default and record it as an explicit assumption in the plan.
21	
22	**Do not** run tests, build the app, or probe runtime behavior in this phase. The goal is a strong plan, not partial execution.
23	
24	### Phase 3: Structure the Plan
25	
26	#### 3.1 Title and File Naming
27	
28	- Draft a clear, searchable title using conventional format such as `feat: Add user authentication` or `fix: Prevent checkout double-submit`
29	- Determine the plan type: `feat`, `fix`, or `refactor`
30	- Build the filename following the repository convention: `<root>/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-HHMM-<type>-<descriptive-name>-plan.md`
31	  - Create `<root>/plans/` if it does not exist
32	  - Take `YYYY-MM-DD-HHMM` from the local wall-clock time at write, so the prefix matches the `date:` frontmatter and the day the user experienced; do not scan for or allocate a daily sequence number
33	  - Reserve the candidate path atomically with exclusive creation; if it already exists, append the smallest available numeric collision suffix (`-2`, `-3`, …) before the extension rather than overwriting it
34	  - Keep the descriptive name concise (3-5 words) and kebab-cased
35	  - Examples: `2026-01-15-0915-feat-user-authentication-flow-plan.md`, `2026-02-03-1642-fix-checkout-race-condition-plan.md`
36	  - Avoid: daily sequence numbers, vague names like "new-feature", and invalid characters (colons, spaces)
37	
38	#### 3.2 Stakeholder and Impact Awareness
39	
40	For **Standard** or **Deep** plans, briefly consider who is affected by this change — end users, developers, operations, other teams — and how that should shape the plan. For cross-cutting work, note affected parties in the System-Wide Impact section.
41	
42	#### 3.3 Break Work into Implementation Units
43	
44	Break the work into logical implementation units. Each unit should represent one meaningful change that an implementer could typically land as an atomic commit.
45	
46	Good units are:
47	- Focused on one component, behavior, or integration seam
48	- Usually touching a small cluster of related files
49	- Ordered by dependency
50	- Concrete enough for execution without pre-writing code
51	
52	Avoid:
53	- 2-5 minute micro-steps
54	- Units that span multiple unrelated concerns
55	- Units that are so vague an implementer still has to invent the plan
56	
57	Each unit carries a stable plan-local **U-ID** assigned in Phase 3.5 (`U1`, `U2`, …). U-IDs survive reordering, splitting, and deletion: new units take the next unused number, gaps are fine, and existing IDs are never renumbered. This lets `ce-work` reference units unambiguously across plan edits.
58	
59	#### 3.4 High-Level Technical Design
60	
61	When the plan's technical approach has shape that prose alone doesn't carry well — architecture across components, sequencing across processes, state machines, branching gates, lifecycles, quantitative comparisons — include a High-Level Technical Design section that conveys the shape. The exact form (component diagram, sequence, swim lane, flowchart, state machine, decision matrix, pseudo-code grammar, bar chart for sizing concerns) is the agent's call per artifact — pick what makes the content land fastest for the reader.
62	
63	See `references/plan-sections.md` for the section catalog including HTD's "include when material" criterion. See the format-rendering reference loaded at Phase 0.0 for how visualizations render in the target format (mermaid in markdown, inline SVG in HTML — with the layout-legibility principles around halo, contrast, and label placement when in HTML).
64	
65	When the plan's approach is a one-paragraph pattern application that prose conveys directly, skip the section. The presence of HTD should earn its keep with content that genuinely benefits from visualization.
66	
67	Plan diagrams render authoritative content alongside the prose — they are not "directional sketches." Do not add hedging captions like *"directional guidance for review, not implementation specification"* to plan diagrams; the prose-is-authoritative rule already governs disagreement, and the hedging weakens the diagram unnecessarily.
68	
69	#### 3.4b Output Structure (Optional)
70	
71	For greenfield plans that create a new directory structure (new plugin, service, package, or module), include an `## Output Structure` section with a file tree showing the expected layout. This gives reviewers the overall shape before diving into per-unit details.
72	
73	**When to include it:**
74	- The plan creates 3+ new files in a new directory hierarchy
75	- The directory layout itself is a meaningful design decision
76	
77	**When to skip it:**
78	- The plan only modifies existing files
79	- The plan creates 1-2 files in an existing directory — the per-unit file lists are sufficient
80	
81	The tree is a scope declaration showing the expected output shape. It is not a constraint — the implementer may adjust the structure if implementation reveals a better layout. The per-unit `**Files:**` sections remain authoritative for what each unit creates or modifies.
82	
83	#### 3.5 Define Each Implementation Unit
84	
85	Each unit is a level-3 heading carrying a stable U-ID prefix matching the format used for R/A/F/AE in requirements docs: `### U1. [Name]`. Number sequentially within the plan starting at U1. Do not render units as bulleted list items or prefix them with `- [ ]` / `- [x]` checkbox markers. List-based unit titles fragment in every standard renderer because the per-unit fields (`**Goal:**`, `**Files:**`, `**Approach:**`, etc.) are written flush-left, which terminates CommonMark list continuation and detaches the fields from the unit they describe. Headings render correctly everywhere, are the right semantic match for sections containing multi-block content, and give each unit an anchor link. The plan is a decision artifact; execution progress is derived from git by `ce-work` rather than stored in the plan body.
86	
87	**Stability rule.** Once assigned, a U-ID is never renumbered. Reordering units leaves their IDs in place (e.g., U1, U3, U5 in their new order is correct; renumbering to U1, U2, U3 is not). Splitting a unit keeps the original U-ID on the original concept and assigns the next unused number to the new unit. Deletion leaves a gap; gaps are fine. This rule matters most during deepening (Phase 5.3), which is the most likely accidental-renumber vector.
88	
89	For each unit, include:
90	- **Goal** - what this unit accomplishes
91	- **Requirements** - which requirements or success criteria it advances (cite R-IDs, and A/F/AE IDs when origin supplies them)
92	- **Dependencies** - what must exist first (cite by U-ID, e.g., "U1, U3")
93	- **Files** - repo-relative file paths to create, modify, or test (never absolute paths)
94	- **Approach** - key decisions, data flow, component boundaries, or integration notes. **Unit-local content only:** cite the governing R-IDs / KTD-IDs for any product or protocol rule rather than restating it. When the content enumerates sequenced steps or per-file changes, write it as a short ordered list under the field label, one step per item — a sentence chaining more than two semicolons is a list wearing a paragraph
95	- **Execution note** - optional natural-language direction, only when the unit benefits from non-default sequencing or proof. Do not treat this as an enum; phrase the evidence the implementer should seek.
96	- **Technical design** - optional pseudo-code or diagram when the unit's approach is non-obvious and prose alone would leave it ambiguous. Frame explicitly as directional guidance, not implementation specification
97	- **Patterns to follow** - existing code or conventions to mirror
98	- **Test scenarios** - enumerate the specific test cases the implementer should write, one scenario per list item (never a semicolon-chained paragraph), right-sized to the unit's complexity and risk. Consider each category below and include scenarios from every category that applies to this unit. A simple config change may need one scenario; a payment flow may need a dozen. The quality signal is specificity — each scenario should name the input, action, and expected outcome so the implementer doesn't have to invent coverage. For units with no behavioral change (pure config, scaffolding, styling), use `Test expectation: none -- [reason]` instead of leaving the field blank. **AE-link convention:** when a test scenario directly enforces an origin Acceptance Example, prefix it with `Covers AE<N>.` (or `Covers F<N> / AE<N>.`). This is sparse-by-design — most test scenarios are finer-grained than AEs and do not link. Do not force AE links onto tests that only cover lower-level implementation details.
99	  - **Happy path behaviors** - core functionality with expected inputs and outputs
100	  - **Edge cases** (when the unit has meaningful boundaries) - boundary values, empty inputs, nil/null states, concurrent access
101	  - **Error and failure paths** (when the unit has failure modes) - invalid input, downstream service failures, timeout behavior, permission denials
102	  - **Integration scenarios** (when the unit crosses layers) - behaviors that mocks alone will not prove, e.g., "creating X triggers callback Y which persists Z". Include these for any unit touching callbacks, middleware, or multi-layer interactions
103	- **Verification** - how an implementer should know the unit is complete, expressed as outcomes rather than shell command scripts
104	
105	Every feature-bearing unit should include the test file path in `**Files:**`.
106	
107	Use `Execution note` sparingly. Good uses include:
108	- `Execution note: Start with a failing integration test for the request/response contract.`
109	- `Execution note: Add characterization coverage before modifying this legacy parser.`
110	- `Execution note: Implement new domain behavior test-first.`
111	- `Execution note: This is mostly packaging/config; prefer install/runtime smoke verification over unit coverage.`
112	
113	Do not expand units into literal `RED/GREEN/REFACTOR` substeps.
114	
115	#### 3.6 Keep Planning-Time and Implementation-Time Unknowns Separate
116	
117	If something is important but not knowable yet, record it explicitly under deferred implementation notes rather than pretending to resolve it in the plan.
118	
119	Examples:
120	- Exact method or helper names
121	- Final SQL or query details after touching real code
122	- Runtime behavior that depends on seeing actual test failures
123	- Refactors that may become unnecessary once implementation starts
124	
125	#### 3.7 Anti-Expansion: Tangential Cleanup and Scope Creep Go to Deferred
126	
127	Distinct from 3.6 (which is about *unknowns* at plan time): 3.7 is about *known but tangential* work that the agent notices while planning but that falls outside the user's confirmed scope. When research surfaces an adjacent refactor, a "while we're here" cleanup, or a scope-adjacent nice-to-have ("we could also add rate limiting"), route it to the existing `### Deferred to Follow-Up Work` subsection in Scope Boundaries (Phase 4.2 Core Plan Template), not into active Implementation Units.
128	
129	This reinforces the synthesis discipline established at Phase 0.7 / Phase 5.1.5 — the user's confirmed scope is what the active plan executes; everything else is deferred. Does NOT impose architectural bias on extend-vs-invent decisions within confirmed scope — that judgment stays with the agent (and is surfaced via the Phase 5.1.5 synthesis when material). The user's explicit ask overrides this default — if the user explicitly requested a refactor, it's in-scope, not deferred.
130	
131	### Phase 4: Write the Plan
132	
133	**NEVER CODE during this skill.** Research, decide, and write the plan — do not start implementation.
134	
135	Use one planning philosophy across all depths. Change the amount of detail, not the boundary between planning and execution.
136	
137	#### 4.1 Plan Depth Guidance
138	
139	**Lightweight**
140	- Keep the plan compact
141	- Usually 2-4 implementation units
142	- Omit optional sections that add little value
143	
144	**Standard**
145	- Use the full core template, omitting optional sections (including High-Level Technical Design) that add no value for this particular work
146	- Usually 3-6 implementation units
147	- Include risks, deferred questions, and system-wide impact when relevant
148	
149	**Deep**
150	- Use the full core template plus optional analysis sections where warranted
151	- Usually 4-8 implementation units
152	- Group units into phases when that improves clarity
153	- Include alternatives considered, documentation impacts, and deeper risk treatment when warranted
154	
155	#### 4.1b Optional Deep Plan Extensions
156	
157	For sufficiently large, risky, or cross-cutting work, add the sections that genuinely help:
158	- **Alternative Approaches Considered**
159	- **Success Metrics** — operational instrumentation for the deep-plan tier: dashboards, error budgets, alert thresholds, and rollout telemetry. A threshold that *is* the product outcome (p95 latency, delivery rate, adoption) belongs to the Product Contract's `### Success Criteria` and never appears here as well; Success Metrics covers only what Success Criteria does not already state. When only one applies, it is almost always Success Criteria.
160	- **Dependencies / Prerequisites**
161	- **Risk Analysis & Mitigation**
162	- **Phased Delivery**
163	- **Documentation Plan**
164	- **Operational / Rollout Notes**
165	- **Future Considerations** only when they materially affect current design
166	
167	Do not add these as boilerplate. Include them only when they improve execution quality or stakeholder alignment.
168	
169	**Alternatives Considered — what to vary.** When this section is included, alternatives must differ on *how* the work is built: architecture, sequencing, boundaries, integration pattern, rollout strategy. Tiny implementation variants (which hash function, which serialization format) belong in Key Technical Decisions, not Alternatives. Product-shape alternatives (different actors, different core outcome, different positioning) belong in `ce-brainstorm`, not here — surface them back upstream rather than re-litigating product questions during planning.
170	
171	#### 4.2 Section Contract and Rendering
172	
173	Compose the plan using two paired references:
174	
175	- `references/plan-sections.md` — the section contract. Describes what the plan contains: the outcome the plan must enable for downstream consumers, the hard floor (Summary, Problem Frame, Requirements, KTDs, Implementation Units), the include-when-material catalog (covering the Product Contract's product-framing sections and the implementation-facing ones; the reference enumerates them), the agency-driven escape hatch (introduce new sections when content warrants), and the ID/content rules.
176	- The format-rendering reference loaded at Phase 0.0 (`markdown-rendering.md` OR `html-rendering.md`) — how to present the sections in the resolved output format.
177	
178	The section catalog is the same regardless of format. Format-specific principles (table-vs-prose by content shape, ID prefix format, diagram rendering, etc.) live in the rendering reference.
179	
180	Omit "include when material" sections that don't carry information for this specific plan. Filling a section with placeholder prose is worse than omitting it.
181	
182	#### 4.3 Planning Rules
183	
184	- **Horizontal rules (`---`) between top-level sections** in Standard and Deep plans, mirroring the `ce-brainstorm` requirements doc convention. Improves scannability of dense plans where many H2 sections sit close together. Omit for Lightweight plans where the whole doc fits on a single screen.
185	- **All file paths must be repo-relative** — never use absolute paths like `/Users/name/Code/project/src/file.ts`. Use `src/file.ts` instead. Absolute paths make plans non-portable across machines, worktrees, and teammates. When a plan targets a different repo than the document's home, state the target repo once at the top of the plan (e.g., `**Target repo:** my-other-project`) and use repo-relative paths throughout
186	- Prefer path plus class/component/pattern references over brittle line numbers
187	- Do not include implementation code — no imports, exact method signatures, or framework-specific syntax
188	- Pseudo-code sketches and DSL grammars are allowed in the High-Level Technical Design section and per-unit technical design fields when they communicate design direction. Frame them explicitly as directional guidance, not implementation specification
189	- Mermaid diagrams are encouraged when they clarify relationships or flows that prose alone would make hard to follow — ERDs for data model changes, sequence diagrams for multi-service interactions, state diagrams for lifecycle transitions, flowcharts for complex branching logic
190	- Do not include git commands, commit messages, or exact test command recipes
191	- Do not expand implementation units into micro-step `RED/GREEN/REFACTOR` instructions
192	- Do not pretend an execution-time question is settled just to make the plan look complete

1	# Plan Sections
2	
3	This reference describes what makes a great implementation plan. It does NOT
4	prescribe how the plan looks on the page — rendering is handled by the
5	format-specific references (`markdown-rendering.md`, `html-rendering.md`).
6	
7	## The outcome
8	
9	A great plan enables three audiences to act:
10	
11	- **The implementing agent** (`ce-work` or a human) starts from an informed
12	  baseline — load-bearing decisions are named, research breadcrumbs orient
13	  their own investigation, unit boundaries are clear. The plan gives the
14	  implementer a starting point, not a substitute for their own investigation.
15	- **The reviewer** identifies the load-bearing decisions and the boundaries
16	  of what's being changed in one pass.
17	- **The future reader** (anyone returning months later) traces why the work
18	  was done, what shaped it, and where the artifacts live.
19	
20	Sections earn their place by serving one of these audiences. Omit padding.
21	
22	## Unified plan artifact contract
23	
24	`ce-plan` writes the canonical compound-engineering plan artifact. The same
25	artifact may begin as a requirements-only skeleton from `ce-brainstorm` and
26	later be enriched by `ce-plan`; it is still one plan file moving through
27	readiness states, not a requirements doc plus a separate implementation doc.
28	
29	When the artifact is meant to be consumed by implementation agents, use:
30	
31	- **`artifact_contract: ce-unified-plan/v1`** — declares this contract.
32	- **`artifact_readiness`** — document completeness, not work progress. Valid
33	  values are:
34	  - `requirements-only` — Product Contract exists; planning sections are not
35	    complete and the artifact is not executable.
36	  - `implementation-ready` — Product Contract, Planning Contract,
37	    Implementation Units, Verification Contract, and Definition of Done are
38	    complete enough for `ce-work`, `/goal`, or an equivalent executor, **and no
39	    launch-blocking open question remains**. A plan that is otherwise complete
40	    but still has a blocking product/architecture question stays
41	    `requirements-only`, so the next step it routes to is blocker resolution /
42	    planning, not implementation. Deferred (non-blocking) questions
43	    do not hold readiness back — mark each open question as blocking or deferred
44	    so this distinction is explicit.
45	- **`product_contract_source`** — where the Product Contract came from:
46	  `ce-brainstorm`, `ce-plan-bootstrap`, `legacy-requirements`, or another
47	  explicit source string when a repo has a specialized producer.
48	- **`execution`** — `code` for implementation plans, `knowledge-work` for
49	  non-code deliverables. Absence remains legacy-compatible and means `code`
50	  only for older plans without `artifact_contract`.
51	
52	Do **not** use progress-like readiness values such as `active`,
53	`in_progress`, `completed`, or `done`. Readiness answers "can the artifact be
54	executed?", not "has execution happened?" Plans still carry no `status` field
55	and no mutable execution lifecycle.
56	
57	Do **not** use `artifact_readiness: approach-plan`. Approach-plans,
58	answer-seeking outputs, and universal-planning outputs are outside this
59	software implementation artifact contract unless they include the full Product
60	Contract, Planning Contract, Implementation Units, Verification Contract, and
61	Definition of Done required for software execution. Route those artifacts by
62	their own shape or by `execution: knowledge-work`, not by adding a third
63	unified readiness value.
64	
65	## Section ID Registry
66	
67	Unified artifacts use these stable logical sections. Markdown uses the
68	heading text; HTML uses matching visible headings and anchor IDs. Downstream
69	skills grep or anchor-scan for these names before reading large bodies.
70	
71	| Logical section | Markdown heading | HTML id | Reader use |
72	|---|---|---|---|
73	| Goal Capsule | `## Goal Capsule` | `goal-capsule` | Objective (outcome), Means (chosen approach), authority hierarchy, and stop conditions |
74	| Product Contract | `## Product Contract` | `product-contract` | Requirements, actors, flows, acceptance examples, product scope |
75	| Product Requirements | `### Requirements` under Product Contract | `product-requirements` | Requirement extraction for review and implementation trace |
76	| Planning Contract | `## Planning Contract` | `planning-contract` | KTDs, technical design, assumptions, sequencing |
77	| Implementation Units | `## Implementation Units` | `implementation-units` | U-ID work packets for execution |
78	| Verification Contract | `## Verification Contract` | `verification-contract` | Repo-specific test commands and quality gates |
79	| Definition of Done | `## Definition of Done` | `definition-of-done` | Global and per-unit completion criteria |
80	| Appendix | `## Appendix` | `appendix` | Long research, raw notes, or supporting detail |
81	
82	Requirements-only artifacts are kept light: a Goal Capsule and the Product
83	Contract. They must not point implementers at absent Planning Contract,
84	Implementation Units, Verification Contract, or Definition of Done sections.
85	`ce-plan` adds those implementation sections when it enriches to
86	implementation-ready. Implementation-ready artifacts include the full registry
87	above, except Appendix remains optional.
88	
89	### Wayfinding: map before reading (size-aware)
90	
91	The document does not carry a reading guide; consuming skills own the reading
92	algorithm. A **short** plan — a lightweight or requirements-only artifact that
93	fits in a screen or two — can just be read in full; that is cheaper and simpler
94	than scanning and ranging. But an implementation-ready unified plan is often
95	long, and HTML output (also supported) is more verbose still, so for anything
96	beyond short, do **not** load the entire artifact to find your way around.
97	Build a section map first, then read only the ranges the task needs:
98	
99	- **Markdown:** scan headings to get the section and unit map — e.g.
100	  `rg -n '^#{1,3} ' <plan>` (top-level sections plus `### U<N>.` units).
101	- **HTML:** scan the heading elements (`<h1>`–`<h3>`) and their anchor ids;
102	  match on the section name and ignore the wrapper tags.
103	
104	In both formats the section **names and anchor ids are the stable contract**
105	from the Section ID Registry above (`Goal Capsule`/`goal-capsule`,
106	`Verification Contract`/`verification-contract`, `### U<N>.` units, …). Wayfind
107	against those registry names, not a brittle tag/format pattern, so the
108	instruction survives rendering changes. After mapping, read metadata, then only
109	the sections the task needs — e.g. Goal Capsule, the active U-ID plus its cited
110	R/F/AE/KTD, Verification Contract, and Definition of Done. Read the Appendix or
111	unrelated units only when a section you are already reading cites them.
112	
113	## Whether a plan file is warranted
114	
115	The kernel's Output Contract gate decides this at intake, before any research: Direct and Chat brief results stay in chat (`references/output-contracts.md`); a Durable run writes the file this reference describes.
116	
117	## Implementation-ready hard floor
118	
119	When an implementation-ready software plan is warranted, these sections are
120	present. They carry the contracts downstream consumers depend on.
121	
122	- **Goal Capsule** — objective, means (only when an approach is fixed),
123	  authority hierarchy, stop conditions, execution profile, and tail
124	  ownership. This is the fastest way for an executor to avoid drifting from
125	  the plan. A reader who has not read the rest of the plan must be able to
126	  hold the Objective as the goal. Remaining-true constraints live on their
127	  owning R-IDs, not as extra Objective clauses — user-checkable is not a
128	  license to pack them onto the Objective. An Objective that is only
129	  understandable after later sections is not yet the Objective, even when a
130	  user could check the outcome and a different implementation would still
131	  serve it. The **Objective** is always the outcome: what is true for users
132	  or operators afterwards, phrased so it would still read as the goal under
133	  a different implementation. It sits outside the component being changed,
134	  which is a question of who can check it rather than of which nouns it
135	  uses: an outcome someone outside that component can verify without knowing
136	  its internals is an Objective even when that component is what changed,
137	  and one only its internals can settle is not the Objective however
138	  outcome-shaped its wording; the registry above decides where it does
139	  belong. The usual failure is an objective about the component's own
140	  execution — the wall-clock it no longer holds, the runtime it no longer
141	  consumes, what stays isolated inside it — which only its internals settle.
142	  Infrastructure and refactor work has such an objective too: the reason
143	  that component's behavior mattered to someone. The chosen approach is the
144	  **Means**, its own line whenever the request or the plan has fixed one —
145	  never invented for outcome-only work. It is a linked projection under the
146	  one-owner rule below: one line naming the approach and citing the KTD or
147	  Key Decision that owns it (`Means: … (KTD2)`), never a restatement of that
148	  owner's mechanism. Test: if the implementation changed, would the
149	  Objective still be the goal, and could a reader who does not know the
150	  changed component's internals tell whether it was met? No to the first
151	  makes it a Means. No to the second means it is stated at the component's
152	  altitude, and the Objective is whatever depended on that component. When a
153	  request supplies only its approach ("move X out of A into B"), that is the
154	  Means; the Objective is the outcome it serves, derived from the request's
155	  motivation, the project's stated problem, or asked for — never the approach
156	  restated.
157	- **Product Contract** — product scope and behavior. Contains Summary, Problem
158	  Frame, Requirements with stable R-IDs, and any material Actors, Flows,
159	  Acceptance Examples, Success Criteria, Scope Boundaries, Dependencies,
160	  Outstanding Questions, and Sources. This replaces the separate requirements
161	  artifact in new brainstorm-to-plan flows.
162	- **Planning Contract** — the implementation-facing decisions: Key Technical
163	  Decisions, high-level design, assumptions, implementation constraints,
164	  sequencing, and research that shapes how the Product Contract will be built.
165	- **Implementation Units** (with stable U-IDs) — discrete work packets sized so
166	  each is independently executable. Each unit names Goal, Requirements,
167	  Files, Approach, Test Scenarios, and Verification. `ce-work` and goal-mode
168	  executors consume these units.
169	  - **Unit Index (large plans only, ~10+ units).** When the plan has roughly
170	    ten or more units, open the section with a compact navigation table — one
171	    row per unit: **U-ID · one-line title · files touched · depends-on**. It
172	    lets an executor map units to files and resolve dependency order without
173	    scanning every unit body. It is a **navigation aid only**: the unit bodies
174	    stay authoritative, it carries nothing beyond those four fields (no
175	    approach, tests, or rationale), and `files touched` is the key/primary
176	    paths, not an exhaustive restatement. **Omit it below ~10 units** — there
177	    the per-unit `Dependencies`/`Files` (and any sequencing or dependency
178	    diagram) already suffice, and an index would be ceremony.
179	- **Verification Contract** — repo-specific commands and quality gates,
180	  including which tests prove the plan, when `release:validate` applies, and
181	  what behavioral skill evaluation is required. Avoid generic "run tests"
182	  language when the repo has concrete commands. When the goal is
183	  optimization-shaped (build time, latency, coverage, bundle size), express a
184	  measurable threshold as the exit criterion (e.g., "p95 latency < 200ms",
185	  "build time reduced 30%") and consider routing to `ce-optimize` — a metric
186	  target is a sharper done signal for a long-running goal than a boolean check.
187	- **Definition of Done** — global and per-unit done criteria. This is the
188	  completion contract for `/goal` or equivalent long-running workflows. Include
189	  a cleanup criterion: a long autonomous run accumulates dead-end and
190	  experimental code from approaches that did not pan out; declaring done
191	  requires that abandoned-attempt code is removed, not left in the diff.
192	
193	## Include when material
194	
195	These sections are present when they carry information that isn't covered
196	elsewhere. The test is not "is this a substantial plan?" — it is
197	*"does this specific plan have content this section would surface?"* Filling
198	a section with placeholder prose is worse than omitting it.
199	
200	The first five entries below carry the Product Contract's product framing —
201	what is being built and why. Later entries mix Product Contract subsections
202	(Scope Boundaries, Open Questions, Acceptance Examples, Sources) with
203	Planning Contract ones; the hard floor above remains authoritative for which
204	section sits under which contract. Problem Frame is unconditional; the other four fire on their own tests. A plan
205	that skips all four conditional framing entries has usually inherited its
206	framing from an upstream Product Contract — check before concluding none of
207	them fire.
208	
209	- **Problem Frame** — the hard floor above contains it unconditionally, so
210	  this entry governs its depth, never whether to include it. Give it
211	  paragraphs when motivation isn't obvious from Summary alone; keep it to a
212	  line or two when the motivation was settled upstream and more would only
213	  echo the origin document. Backward-looking / situational. Does NOT restate
214	  the proposal; the remedy lives in Summary.
215	
216	- **Key Decisions** — include when the plan carries product-level choices
217	  that constrain the Requirements below, whether made during planning (scope
218	  narrowings, defaults chosen against a real alternative, framing the user
219	  picked) or inherited from an upstream Product Contract, which Phase 0.3
220	  requires carrying forward with its rationale. Each entry is a provenance
221	  index entry, not a second statement of the rule: the decision in bold, at
222	  most one line of rationale, and exact `Governs R5, R7` links when it
223	  constrains specific requirements. The normative text lives on the governed
224	  Rs. Session-settled annotations follow the rules under "ID and content
225	  rules" below. Distinct from Planning Contract's Key Technical Decisions,
226	  which record how-level choices; a product decision belongs here, and a KTD
227	  cites it rather than mirroring it. Skip only when no such
228	  choice exists on any side: every requirement follows directly from the
229	  request, any upstream Product Contract weighed no alternatives, and the
230	  session settled none. A `session-settled:` decision always keeps the
231	  section — plan-write and the routing table both require its labeled entry
232	  to live here.
233	
234	- **Success Criteria** — include when there are quality / metric / handoff
235	  signals that Requirements don't already carry: quantitative metrics ("p95
236	  latency under 200ms"), qualitative criteria ("the agent's output reads as
237	  one voice"), process / handoff quality ("ce-doc-review can act on this
238	  without follow-ups"). Skip when Requirements ARE the success criteria
239	  (every R is "done when the R is true"). Requirements that describe an
240	  approach rather than an outcome are not success criteria; then include at
241	  least one criterion that would show the Goal Capsule Objective was reached.
242	
243	- **Actors** — include when the work has multi-party behavior (multiple
244	  humans, agents, or systems meaningfully involved) that the units must
245	  honor. Skip for single-actor work and for plans whose change is internal
246	  to one component — most implementation plans skip this.
247	
248	- **Key Flows** — include when the work has multi-step behavior whose
249	  sequencing the units must preserve. Skip when the change is not
250	  flow-shaped, or when Requirements and Acceptance Examples together already
251	  prevent downstream invention of paths — again, most implementation plans
252	  skip this.
253	
254	- **High-Level Technical Design** — include when the technical approach has
255	  shape that prose alone doesn't carry well: architecture across components,
256	  sequencing across processes, state machines, branching gates.
257	  Visualizations (component topology, sequence, swim lane, flowchart,
258	  data-flow) typically live here. Skip when the approach is a one-paragraph
259	  pattern application that the prose itself conveys.
260	
261	- **Scope Boundaries** — include when scope is contested, when there are
262	  tempting non-goals worth naming explicitly, or when "deferred for later"
263	  needs distinguishing from "outside the product's identity." Skip when scope
264	  is obvious from Requirements alone.
265	
266	- **Open Questions** — include when there are genuinely unresolved items that
267	  block planning or implementation. Skip when the plan is complete; an empty
268	  "Open Questions: none" section signals false uncertainty.
269	
270	- **System-Wide Impact** — include when the change affects cross-cutting
271	  concerns (data lifecycles, auth boundaries, performance posture, cardinal
272	  rules, shared infrastructure, agent/tool parity, prompt context, shared
273	  workspaces). Skip for changes localized to one component where the impact is
274	  self-evident.
275	
276	- **Risks & Dependencies** — include when there are real risks worth flagging
277	  (external service changes, version pins under churn, behavioral assumptions
278	  worth highlighting) or material upstream dependencies. Skip for low-risk
279	  localized work.
280	
281	- **Acceptance Examples** — include when any requirement has a state-dependent
282	  or conditional shape ("When X, Y") where the prose alone leaves ambiguity
283	  about edge cases. Skip when all requirements are unconditional and
284	  unambiguous.
285	
286	- **Documentation / Operational Notes** — include when documentation,
287	  monitoring, runbooks, or rollout steps need explicit notes. Skip when the
288	  work is purely internal and uses existing operational scaffolding without
289	  modification.
290	
291	- **Sources / Research** — surface the research that orients the implementer
292	  or justifies load-bearing choices. The test: *"if I were the implementer
293	  reading this cold, would this breadcrumb help me make better choices?"*
294	  Yes → surface (code locations like `services/convex/reports.ts:174-176`,
295	  external docs, RFCs, constraints, prior plans — the category is inclusive,
296	  not enumerated). Process exhaust (reading the user's prompt, glancing at
297	  obvious entry points, restating prose) → omit. Surface inline next to the
298	  KTD or unit it justifies, or as a dedicated section — both shapes work.
299	
300	## Agent agency
301	
302	The catalog is a floor, not a ceiling. When the plan's content doesn't fit
303	any catalog section, introduce a new one — don't force the content into a
304	section it doesn't belong in. Content drives section choices, not vice
305	versa.
306	
307	The agent also picks per artifact:
308	
309	- Whether Problem Frame merges into Summary — legacy and non-unified plans
310	  only. Any `ce-unified-plan/v1` artifact keeps both headings regardless of
311	  plan depth: the hard floor names them separately and downstream consumers
312	  anchor on them. (Scoped by artifact contract, not by depth — a `Lightweight`
313	  plan can still be implementation-ready.)
314	- Sub-groupings (Requirements by capability, KTDs by component, Units phased
315	  into milestones)
316	- How much detail each section carries
317	- Whether HTD has one diagram, several, or none — and whether visualizations
318	  live in HTD or embedded in other sections

320	## Prose economy
321	
322	"Include when material" sizes *which* sections appear; this sizes *how the kept
323	prose reads*. A section can be material and still be written loosely — the
324	failure mode is a material section padded into a wall of text where
325	contradictions hide and the implementing agent loses the thread. A deep plan
326	earns length through coverage (more units, more traced requirements, real
327	risks), never through wordiness around that coverage.
328	
329	Hold every kept section to these:
330	
331	- **Lead with the decision or outcome.** Put the conclusion first, then the
332	  reason, then background; keep one claim plus its support per paragraph. Don't
333	  bury a Key Technical Decision, the chosen scope, an open blocker, or a unit
334	  goal beneath its rationale. This does not override section roles — Summary
335	  stays proposal-only, Problem Frame stays motivation-only and never restates
336	  the remedy.
337	- **Use an ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (STE)-inspired style for
338	  technical plan content.** Write short, direct sentences. Keep one decision,
339	  action, or condition per sentence, and use one consistent term for each
340	  concept. Preserve exact identifiers, paths, commands, protocol names, and
341	  domain terms. Shorten sentences, not content: preserve every distinct
342	  requirement, qualification, and test scenario. A Summary is a handful of
343	  sentences, not one sentence with five semicolons and four parentheticals. A
344	  KTD's rationale is the load-bearing reason, not every reason.
345	- **A requirement or unit is one sentence of intent plus at most one
346	  qualifier.** When it would specify two outcomes ("either A or B, the
347	  implementer decides"), state the intent and send the fork to Open Questions —
348	  don't write both arms in full inside the item.
349	- **Cut hedges and intensifiers.** "Critically", "deliberately", "explicitly",
350	  "genuinely", "actually", "simply" carry nothing the implementer acts on.
351	- **Prefer the verb to the nominalization.** "Demote the grid", not "the
352	  demotion of the grid is the deliberate change in this plan".
353	
354	Precision is not padding: keep file paths, IDs, dates, domain terms,
355	conditionals, and exact thresholds verbatim; when a concrete anchor is knowable
356	from the work already done, use it instead of a vague abstraction. Economy
357	targets the connective tissue around precision, never the precision itself.
358	
359	**Resolve in place; don't stratify.** When deepening, a doc-review pass, or a
360	later decision supersedes earlier text, rewrite or remove the original — don't
361	leave it standing as strikethrough or stack a separate "resolutions" layer on
362	top of it. Version control holds the history. Stacked strata double the reading
363	surface and hide which text is live.
364	
365	**One owner per rule; cite, don't restate.** A normative rule — a gate, cap,
366	threshold, protocol, or output contract — is stated in full at exactly one
367	owning entry: product behavior on its R-ID; an implementation choice on its
368	KTD. Every other layer cites the owning ID and adds only what is local to
369	it — a unit's Approach carries unit-local deltas (files, sequencing,
370	patterns), never a re-derivation of the protocol its cited Rs and KTDs own.
371	Linked projections are sanctioned (an AE restating behavior under
372	`Covers R…`, a Flow citing the Rs it sequences). **Unlinked sibling
373	restatement** — the same rule written out again in a KTD, Scope bullet, or
374	Approach with no ID link — is the defect: each copy drifts independently.
375	When linked layers disagree, authority is typed: the **R wins on product
376	behavior**; the **KTD wins on implementation mechanism** within its cited R
377	constraints; a unit overrides neither; AEs and Flows illustrate and
378	sequence, never amend.
379	
380	**Bind external authorities; don't summarize them.** When a requirement,
381	KTD, or unit adopts an external document (a field guide, spec, standard),
382	state the commitment, cite the path, and record only this work's deltas. A
383	multi-sentence summary of the cited document is restatement of an owner that
384	lives outside the doc.
385	
386	**Named test, run before the plan is declared written:** could the implementer
387	find a contradiction in each section in one pass? Could a colleague who was
388	not in the session say what this work is after the Objective alone? A sentence
389	carrying more than one parenthetical, a sentence chaining more than two
390	semicolons, an item specifying two outcomes, or a rule stated in full in more than one section
391	fails the test — split it (a semicolon chain becomes a list), defer it, or
392	replace the duplicate with its owning ID.
393	
394	## Plan metadata fields
395	
396	Every plan carries a small set of stable metadata fields that downstream
397	tooling depends on. The contract is format-independent: in markdown these
398	fields appear as YAML frontmatter at the top of the file; in HTML they
399	appear as visible header text (typically a `<dl>` of `<dt>`/`<dd>` pairs or
400	a stats strip). Field names and semantics are the same across both formats
401	so consumers can locate them without knowing which format produced the
402	plan.
403	
404	### Required
405	
406	- **`title`** — the plan's descriptive name with a ` - Plan` suffix
407	  (e.g., `Highlighter Tool - Plan`), matching the H1 (markdown) or document
408	  `<h1>` (HTML) so file metadata and visible heading don't drift. Stable
409	  across readiness states (it is a plan at every stage). Do not put a
410	  conventional-commit prefix (`feat:`/`fix:`) in the title — the `type` field
411	  carries that classification.
412	- **`type`** — conventional-commit-prefix-aligned classification (`feat`,
413	  `fix`, `refactor`, `chore`, `docs`, `perf`, `test`, etc.). Carries the
414	  intent the eventual commit message should reflect.
415	- **`date`** — creation date in ISO 8601 (`YYYY-MM-DD`), ASCII digits only.
416	
417	Plans carry **no `status` field** — a plan is a decision artifact, not a
418	tracked work item. `ce-work` does not mutate the plan at ship time;
419	whether a plan shipped is derived from git, not stored in the doc. Do not
420	add a `status` field or an `active → completed` lifecycle.
421	
422	### Optional but well-known
423	
424	These fields are not required, but when set they have fixed names and
425	semantics so downstream tooling can rely on them:
426	
427	- **`origin`** — repo-relative path to an upstream brainstorm requirements
428	  doc (e.g., `docs/brainstorms/2026-05-12-pagination-requirements.md`).
429	  Set when planning from an upstream brainstorm; carried for traceability
430	  and re-resolved when `ce-plan` re-deepens.
431	- **`deepened`** — ISO 8601 date marking the first time the confidence
432	  check substantively strengthened the plan. Presence affects Phase 0.1
433	  resume fast-path logic (see `references/deepening-workflow.md`).
434	- **`execution`** — execution domain for downstream routing: `code`
435	  (the default when absent) or `knowledge-work`. `ce-work`'s input triage
436	  reads this: a plan marked `execution: knowledge-work` routes to the
437	  non-code carve-out (read sources, synthesize, produce a deliverable —
438	  skipping the branch/test/commit/CI lifecycle); absent or `code` routes
439	  to the normal code path. Written by `ce-plan`'s approach-altitude flow
440	  (`references/approach-altitude.md`) when a non-code deliverable is
441	  persisted for execution.
442	
443	Field names are stable across plan revisions — never rename a field or
444	repurpose its semantics. Agents composing new plans MUST use these exact
445	names; adding new fields is fine, but renaming `origin` to `source` or
446	`date` to `created` breaks the downstream consumers above.
447	
448	## ID and content rules
449	
450	These apply regardless of rendering format.
451	
452	- **Stable IDs.** R-IDs (Requirements), U-IDs (Implementation Units),
453	  KTD-IDs (Key Technical Decisions, implementation-ready plans), A-IDs
454	  (if Actors fire), F-IDs (if Flows fire), AE-IDs (if Acceptance Examples
455	  fire). IDs are stable across plan revisions — never renumber to "clean
456	  up gaps."
457	- **Plain prefix.** `R1.`, `U1.`, `KTD1.` as bullet prefixes. Do not bold;
458	  the prefix is visually distinctive on its own.
459	- **KTD-IDs on implementation-ready plans.** Number Key Technical Decisions
460	  (`KTD1.`, next unused number, same never-renumber rule as U-IDs) in newly
461	  authored implementation-ready plans, and in an existing plan whenever a
462	  KTD is added, split, or first cited by a unit. Untouched unnumbered KTDs
463	  in legacy plans stay as they are — readable by label, no mass renumbering.
464	- **Repo-relative paths.** Always. Never absolute paths in plan content;
465	  they break portability across machines, worktrees, teammates.
466	- **No process exhaust.** No "captured at Phase X" notes, no `## Next Steps`
467	  pointing to the next skill, no italic provenance lines. Engineering process
468	  metadata belongs in commit messages and tool output, not the artifact.
469	- **Session-settled annotations on KTDs.** A Key Technical Decision that
470	  records a decision settled in the invoking conversation carries an inline
471	  annotation on its entry:
472	  `(session-settled: user-directed — chosen over <alternative>: <one-line reason>)`.
473	  Exactly two classes: `user-directed` (the user chose against or between
474	  surfaced options) and `user-approved` (the agent proposed with the tradeoff
475	  surfaced; the user assented). An agent never labels its own unexamined
476	  proposal. A KTD that makes the how-level choice instantiating a labeled
477	  Product Contract Key Decision inherits the label and cites the decision's
478	  governed R-IDs. Do **not** create a KTD that merely mirrors a Product Key
479	  Decision with no new technical choice — the Key Decision plus its
480	  `Governs R…` links already own that content. The annotation is
481	  self-contained — decision, rejected alternative, and one-line reason
482	  readable without the conversation — and lives inline on the entry: no
483	  sidecar files, no frontmatter registry, no numeric weights, no lifecycle
484	  field. Like a `(see origin: <path>)` citation, it is decision provenance,
485	  not process exhaust — review passes must not strip it. A consumer that
486	  does not recognize the annotation treats the entry as a normal KTD.
487	- **Group Requirements by concern when they span distinct logical areas.**
488	  The trigger is distinct concerns, not item count — even four requirements
489	  benefit from grouping if they cover three different topics. Skip grouping
490	  only when all requirements are genuinely about the same thing; a long flat
491	  list is a smell that subgroups were missed. Group by capability (e.g.,
492	  "Packaging", "Migration and compatibility", "Contributor workflow"), not by
493	  the order requirements were discussed. R-IDs stay continuous across groups
494	  (R1, R2 in the first group; R3, R4 in the second; never restart at R1 per
495	  group).

502	- **Markdown rendering:** `references/markdown-rendering.md`
503	- **HTML rendering:** `references/html-rendering.md`

505	This reference (`plan-sections.md`) is about WHAT the plan contains;
